source.title: Grokking Explained: A Statistical Phenomenon
source.authors: Breno W. Carvalho; A. S. d'Avila Garcez; L. Lamb; Emilio Vital Brazil

record.file_problem: Some equation and figure text is garbled in the extraction; the main text and appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests delayed generalization using new, non-algorithmic datasets and controlled data-distribution shifts, rather than reproducing the original modular-arithmetic experiments.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own grokking results for synthetic class/subclass datasets and makes an explicit statement about MNIST. Prior-work results are not included as rows. Learning-rate and weight-decay settings are experimental setup, not outcome rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own delayed-generalization curves on synthetic Gaussian class/subclass data, which bear on V3's non-algorithmic part. It argues that train–test distribution shift, not sparsity or regularization, is the cause, which restates V3's 'regime, not data' framing. Init scale (8) and weight decay (1e-4) are fixed throughout, so the regime switch itself is never varied.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude grokking is mainly a statistical, distribution-shift phenomenon arising from class/subclass sampling. They hold that small samples, regularization and initialization amplify it but do not define it. They report it can occur with dense data, find late generalization largely architecture-independent, and call for new stopping criteria.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses synthetic Gaussian class/subclass datasets with controlled sampling shifts and an MNIST clustering experiment, rather than the original small algorithmic datasets. It evaluates MLPs and a 2-layer Transformer.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with subclass structure and sampling: removing a subclass prevents grokking in the equidistant dataset but not the equivariant dataset; smaller samples increase reported grokking intensity. The study states that the tested learning rate was 10^-3, weight decay 10^-4, and initialization scale factor 8.

fits_no_version.finding: Grokking intensity is attributed to train–test distribution shift created by subclass under-sampling. Subclass proximity (equivariant structure) lets grokking occur even with a subclass absent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking-like delay is driven by train–test distribution shift; data sparsity matters only as one way of producing that shift.

record.problems: Results are aggregated from 10 independent runs, but uncertainty estimates are not stated. The study does not identify how long training may need to continue before late generalization. The supplied text gives limited detail about MNIST outcomes and condition-specific Transformer results.
record.rows_left_out: No reported outcome rows omitted. Condition-specific Transformer results and detailed MNIST results are not stated in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Text and molecule data. Switching grokking on or off through initialization scale or weight norm: init scale is fixed at 8 and weight decay at 1e-4. Any MNIST result is unreported.
Not tested: no mechanism or progress measures.
Not tested: weight decay is not varied, and no critical dataset size or ungrokking is examined.

missing.what: Condition-specific 2-layer Transformer results said to be in Appendix A; that appendix has no such results in the text
MNIST clustered-shift grokking outcomes (curves, model, any numbers)

record.verdict_notes: No uncertainty is reported, and results are qualitative averages over 10 runs. Every run uses initialization scale 8, the large-init setting Liu et al. use to induce grokking, so data effects are measured inside a grokking-prone regime and cannot be separated from it. Delay length is not measured; ΔS measures intensity. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test the claim on small algorithmic datasets or report how delay changes as an algorithmic training set shrinks.
It does not measure the formation of a generalizing circuit, memorizing components, or continuous mechanism-level progress.
It tests grokking-like behavior on synthetic non-algorithmic data and reports an MNIST experiment, but does not test text or molecules, or switch grokking through initialization scale or weight norm.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is tested.
Weight decay is not varied as a causal intervention; the study does not measure circuit efficiency or test a predicted critical dataset size or ungrokking below it.
The study does not identify or compare algorithms learned across runs.
Optimizer-instability and floating-point/softmax-artifact explanations are not tested.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.operation_detail: Train on balanced samples while varying dataset size.

conditions.value: varied; individual sizes not stated here

rows.measure: Test-set performance over training; grokking intensity
rows.value: Grokking occurs in every tested case; its intensity increases as dataset size decreases.
rows.note: The paper reports average test-set curves after training loss has converged; individual curve values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: The Fig 3a caption says grokking 'occurs in every case'. Section 5.2 says it exists 'only' at considerably small sample sizes. These conflict. The measure is grokking intensity (ΔS), not the length of the delay. No numbers are given.

source_check.problem: The value matches Figure 3a's caption, but Section 5.2 contradicts its universal wording by restricting grokking to considerably small sample sizes.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.operation_detail: Train with a selected subclass removed entirely.
rows.value: Removing a subclass completely prevents grokking; the models remain on a sub-optimal plateau.
rows.note: The paper contrasts this setting with adding back a small number of examples.
rows.check: Correct. With the training regime unchanged, removing a subclass leaves models on a sub-optimal plateau with no late generalization.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.2, unbalanced equidistant subclass sampling; Figure 3b caption.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.operation_detail: Train after adding a small number of examples back to the selected subclass.
rows.value: Adding back 20% of subclass examples enables grokking within the same maximum number of epochs and with the same number of samples.
rows.note: The text also says that even a very small fraction, for example f=0.01, can allow late generalization.
rows.check: The f=0.2 value comes from the caption. The text cites f=0.01 as enough. Only qualitative curves are available.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 3b caption states 20%, matched sample counts and maximum epochs; Section 5.2 separately gives f=0.01.
